title_en: Unexpected Item in the Bagging Area
description_ru: Юмористический рассказ о войне человека с кассой самообслуживания, которая подозревает его во всём, включая собственное существование.
text:
I would like it known that I entered the supermarket in a spirit of generosity. It was a Tuesday evening, the sort of grey and indeterminate hour at which the human being, having completed the day's labours, is prepared to forgive almost anything, and my intentions were modest: a loaf of bread, a lemon and a small tub of hummus. Three items. A grown man ought to be able to buy three items without incident. That, at any rate, was my theory, and I mention it here because it was the last time that I was right about anything that evening.

The store had recently abolished most of its human cashiers, replaced, in a ceremony that I imagine was attended by no one, with a row of cheerful grey machines called Self-Service Stations. A single young employee in a lanyard, whose job description seemed to consist of hovering near the machines and looking apologetic, gestured towards one of them with the gloomy courtesy of a funeral director. "It's very intuitive," he said, in a voice that suggested he had not been consulted. I thanked him and approached the machine, which greeted me with a tone of such sugary warmth that I knew at once I was in trouble.

"Welcome," it said. "Please scan your first item." I scanned the bread. The machine emitted a small, pleased chirp, rather like a bird that has swallowed a bicycle bell. I placed the bread in the bagging area. "Please scan your next item," it said. I scanned the lemon, which weighs perhaps a hundred grams and was, I should point out, labelled with a sticker clearly identifying it as a lemon. The machine considered this for a moment. Then it announced, in a flat and lofty voice, "Unexpected item in the bagging area."

I looked at the bagging area. In it lay the bread, the lemon, my elbow and a faint sense of injustice. "There is nothing unexpected," I said, aloud, to a machine, in a supermarket, with the carefully reasonable tone of a man assuring a customs officer that he has nothing to declare. "I have just scanned them." The machine said nothing, and flashed a red light, which in the language of such devices is understood to mean "I am not angry, I am merely disappointed." A queue, I noticed, had begun to form behind me, and a woman at the front was assessing me, over the top of her shopping basket, in the manner of a magistrate.

I removed the lemon. The machine said: "Please place the item in the bagging area." I put it back. "Unexpected item in the bagging area," it said. I removed the bread, which seemed to be the source of the trouble. "Please place the item in the bagging area." I returned it. "Unexpected item in the bagging area." By now I had the lurid sensation of being trapped in an existential play, in which a man and a machine are engaged in an eternal dialogue about the meaning of a lemon. I began to sweat. The queue behind me began to sigh.

At this point, the young man in the lanyard came over, slowly, as one approaches a wounded bear, and inserted a small card into the side of the machine. A moment later, the screen turned green, the red light vanished and the machine, in a tone of sublime forgiveness, declared: "Approved. Please continue." The young man gave me a look of weary solidarity, and withdrew. I gazed at the machine with new respect. It had humbled me, then pardoned me, in a single manoeuvre, with the practised elegance of a minor aristocrat.

I scanned the hummus. "Please wait for assistance," said the machine. I had, I realised, been placed in a sort of probation. The tub was inspected, with ceremony, by the assistant, who looked at it, looked at me and looked at the machine, and then, with a long and expressive sigh, tapped the screen. "It thinks you've got a different hummus," he said. "How different?" I asked. "That's the thing," he said, "it won't say." We stood for a moment in contemplative silence, united by the inscrutability of the infinite.

When it came to payment, I tapped my card. "Card declined," said the machine. I tapped it again. "Card declined." I knew, with perfect certainty, that I had money, as I had checked my balance that morning with the numb dread that is the modern equivalent of prayer. I tried a second card, which was declined with even greater disdain. At this stage I abandoned my dignity and inserted the card in the slot, as one might insert a coin into a fountain in the hope of a wish. The machine, in an access of benevolence, accepted it. "Thank you for shopping with us," it said. "Please take your receipt."

I took my receipt. It was nearly a metre long, printed with the details of my purchase and, in the generous margins, a sequence of coupons for products that I had no wish to buy, together with a request that I should "tell us how we did." I looked at it for a long time. Then I took my bread, my lemon and my hummus, now emotionally compromised, and walked, with great deliberateness, towards the exit, where a security gate watched me with the expression of a sceptical bouncer.

The gate, I am relieved to say, let me through. Outside, in the car park, the evening was cool and quiet, and a light rain had begun to fall. I stood for a moment in the drizzle, and felt a rush of gratitude, quite out of proportion to the occasion, for the sheer reliability of the weather. It did not ask me to wait for assistance. It did not suspect me of anything. It simply rained, upon the just and the unjust alike, and expected nothing in return.

I have thought about the experience a good deal since. I have wondered whether the machine and I might have misunderstood one another, and whether, in some alternate arrangement, we might have been friends. But I do not think so. Last week, I went back, and I observed an elderly lady in front of me buying a single banana. "Unexpected item in the bagging area," said the machine. She regarded it calmly, took the banana in her hand and ate it, then and there, with great composure. "Not any longer," she said.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Короткий центральный гласный; рот чуть приоткрыт, губы расслаблены; не заменяйте на русское «о».
Короткий звук, близкий к русскому «э», но рот чуть закрытее; не растягивайте.
Кончик языка между зубами, голос включён; не заменяйте на «з» или «д».
Конечные звонкие d, b, g произносите с голосом, а не оглушайте: «card» не должно звучать как «карт».

questions.question: What three items did the narrator want to buy?
questions.answer: A loaf of bread, a lemon and a small tub of hummus.

questions.question: What did the machine keep saying?
How did the assistant fix the problem?
questions.answer: He inserted a small card into the machine.

questions.question: What did the elderly lady do with her banana?
questions.answer: She ate it on the spot.
